section_title: Where did Jerusalem’s beauty and honor come from?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 Then I passed by and saw you, and you were indeed old enough for love. So I spread My cloak over you and covered your nakedness. I pledged Myself to you, entered into a covenant with you, and you became Mine, declares the Lord GOD. 9 Then I bathed you with water, rinsed off your blood, and anointed you with oil. 10 I clothed you in embroidered cloth and gave you sandals of fine leather. I wrapped you in fine linen and covered you with silk.

11 I adorned you with jewelry, and I put bracelets on your wrists and a chain around your neck. 12 I put a ring in your nose, earrings on your ears, and a beautiful crown upon your head. 13 So you were adorned with gold and silver, and your clothing was made of fine linen, silk, and embroidered cloth. You ate fine flour, honey, and oil. You became very beautiful and rose to be queen. 14 Your fame spread among the nations on account of your beauty, for it was perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you, declares the Lord GOD.

context_lines: The story moves from rescue to covenant. The Lord spreads His cloak over the young woman, pledges Himself to her and declares that she has become His. He bathes, anoints, clothes and adorns her.
The food, garments and jewelry are gifts. She becomes beautiful, rises to be queen and gains fame among the nations, but the Lord explains the source of that splendor: He bestowed it on her.

The cloak also appears in [Ruth 3:6–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ruth/3.htm), where Ruth asks Boaz to spread his garment over her because he is a kinsman-redeemer. In Ezekiel, the oath and covenant make the marriage picture explicit.
This account of generous provision prepares for the accusation that follows. Jerusalem cannot explain its later success as something achieved independently of the One who rescued and cared for it.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/16.htm) and the [Cambridge commentary on verse 8](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/ezekiel/16.htm) connect the marriage covenant with Israel’s deliverance from Egypt and covenant at Sinai. Henry’s account of the chapter likewise treats the provision and marriage as God’s generous dealings with His people.
The details build one main picture: the city’s beauty and standing were received. The Lord’s gifts called for a faithful response, rather than pride in possessions or reputation.
god_plan_lines: [Ephesians 5:25–32](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/5.htm) describes Christ loving the church and giving Himself for her, cleansing her and presenting her in glory. The passage uses the marriage picture to explain Christ’s self-giving care.

This is a biblical parallel, rather than an explicit quotation of Ezekiel 16. In both pictures, the beloved’s splendor depends on what the Lord gives. Ephesians develops the theme through Christ’s sacrifice and His purpose to make His people holy, and calls husbands to nourishing, cherishing love.
